chapter_title: Advanced Identity and Access Management (IAM) Patterns

screens.title: Advanced IAM Patterns
screens.subtitle: Cross-account roles, federation (SAML/OIDC), and ABAC for scalable security

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn three professional IAM patterns that reduce risk and operational overhead. First, cross-account IAM roles let one account assume a role in another account to perform actions without long-lived credentials. Second, identity federation through SAML or OpenID Connect allows corporate identities and modern identity platforms to grant users or applications temporary AWS credentials. Third, ABAC moves authorization from static roles to dynamic attributes, enabling large organizations to scale permissions by tagging principals and resources. Each pattern replaces brittle workarounds—like duplicated user accounts or static keys—with temporary credentials and policy-driven controls. You will see concrete JSON trust and permissions examples that implement these patterns, a practical hands-on scenario for creating a read-only auditor role, and common mistakes to avoid, such as overly permissive trust policies or inconsistent tagging. By the end, you should be able to design a secure trust relationship between accounts, choose federation options for humans or machines, and apply ABAC policies that simplify permission management. Think about which of these patterns would reduce credential sprawl in your environment and why short-lived sessions are central to secure cross-account access.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use temporary, well-scoped credentials—via cross-account roles, federation, or ABAC—to reduce long-lived keys and simplify large-scale permission management.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you will develop four practical competencies. First, you will implement cross-account access using IAM roles so one account can safely assume a role in another without shared long-lived credentials. Practice here matters because it eliminates static keys and centralizes control. Second, you will integrate AWS with external identity providers using SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect. You will understand the flow of assertions and tokens and why federated sign-on centralizes authentication and enforces corporate policies like MFA. Third, you will design and apply attribute-based access control strategies. ABAC uses tags on principals and resources to scale permissions across many projects, reducing role and policy sprawl. Fourth, you will identify and mitigate common IAM security risks, such as overly permissive trust policies, wildcard principals, and inconsistent tagging. Each objective includes a milestone so you can verify competence: creating a cross-account role, configuring a SAML trust, writing an ABAC policy with resource and principal tags, and finding trust-policy misconfigurations. These skills help you build secure, maintainable AWS environments at scale.

narration.text: Now let's focus on how you will apply and verify each objective. For cross-account roles, practice creating a role that a specific account role can assume, attach a least-privilege permissions policy, and test role assumption with the AWS CLI. Verify you cannot escalate privileges beyond read-only when assumed. For federation, configure a SAML provider or an OIDC provider in IAM, create a role trusting that provider, and validate browser sign-on or token exchange for a service account. screens.title: Cross-account IAM roles
screens.subtitle: What an assume-role trust relationship is and why it replaces shared credentials

narration.text: Cross-account IAM roles let one AWS account grant temporarily scoped permissions to an entity from another account without distributing long-lived credentials. In practice, the trusted account defines a role and attaches two things: a trust policy that lists who may assume the role, and a permissions policy that specifies what the assumed role can do. When an entity in the trusting account calls the security token service to assume the role, STS returns temporary credentials that expire automatically. This pattern matters because it centralizes access control, reduces credential sprawl, and enables auditability through short sessions. A concrete example is a centralized Security Audit account that assumes a read-only role in multiple workload accounts to list EC2 instances for compliance checks. A common misconception is that assuming a role grants permissions beyond what the role's permissions policy allows; in reality, the assumed session is bounded by the role's permissions and any session policies applied by the caller. Key takeaway: design trust policies narrowly—scope the Principal to exact roles or ARNs and avoid wildcard Principals. Try to include an external ID or require MFA where trust spans organizational boundaries to reduce risk.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A trust relationship plus a permissions policy that yields temporary credentials when assumed by an allowed principal.

content.html:
Core Concept

Cross-account IAM roles

A role in one account can be assumed by a specific principal in another account, yielding temporary credentials from STS.

Why this matters
Eliminates long-lived credentials, centralizes auditing, and restricts access using temporary sessions.
Common misconception
Assumed permissions are not additive with the caller's original permissions; the session is limited by the role's policy and any session policies.
Key Takeaway

Scope trust policies to specific ARNs and prefer temporary sessions over shared keys for cross-account access.

Annotated trust relationship example
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_A_ID:root"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
Example scenario
Central Security account assumes a read-only role in each workload account for inventory and compliance checks.
Pro tip
Refine the Principal to a role ARN rather than the entire account root to enforce least privilege.

screens.title: Trust policy JSON walk-through
screens.subtitle: Understanding the Principal, Action, and conditions in a trust policy

narration.text: Let's walk through the parts of a trust policy and why each matters. A trust policy has statements similar to an access policy, but it is attached to a role and answers the question: who is allowed to assume this role? The Principal element specifies the entity that may assume the role; it can be an account, a specific IAM role, a federated provider, or an AWS service. The Action is almost always sts:AssumeRole for cross-account roles, but when using SAML it becomes sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML. Conditions tighten who or when a principal can assume the role—for example checking the SAML audience or requiring a source IP, or an external ID. A concrete example from the chapter shows permitting Account A's root; a better pattern refines that to a specific role ARN inside Account A. A common mistake is leaving Principal as a wildcard or the account root, which grants broad ability to assume the role. Takeaway: keep Principals specific and add Conditions such as external IDs or MFA where appropriate to reduce risk. Trust policy JSON walk-through means principal identifies who may assume the role, action signals the assume method, and conditions add extra constraints like audience or external id.. In practical terms, understanding the principal, action, and conditions in a trust policy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trust policy anatomy
keyIdea.text: Principal identifies who may assume the role, Action signals the assume method, and Conditions add extra constraints like audience or external ID.

content.html:
Trust policy example
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_A_ID:role/CentralSecurityAuditor"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
Principal
Specify the exact role ARN or federated provider to limit who may assume the role.
Condition
Add external ID, source IP, or assertion audience checks for extra assurance.
Why refine Principals?
  • Restrict assume-role to a specific role ARN inside the trusting account.
  • Prevent accidental broad access from account-wide principals.
  • Make audits and incident investigation straightforward when Principal is explicit.
Common mistake

Using Principal: { "AWS": "*" } or an account root ARN gives broad assume permissions and is a frequent security hole.

screens.title: Cross-account use cases and flows
screens.subtitle: Common patterns: centralized security, CI/CD deployment, and service access

narration.text: Cross-account roles enable several recurring patterns: centralized security auditing, CI/CD pipelines deploying to multiple accounts, and delegated service access for automation. In a centralized security pattern, an audit account assumes a role in each workload account with read-only permissions. In CI/CD, the build account's pipeline assumes a deploy role in target accounts to perform controlled deployments. For service-level delegation, an AWS service or managed workflow in one account may assume a role in another to access resources like S3 or KMS. The process is similar across patterns: create the role in the target account, set a narrow trust policy permitting the exact principal or role in the caller account, attach least-privilege permissions, then call STS to assume the role and use temporary credentials. A common misconception is that cross-account assume-role is only for humans—it's equally important for services and pipelines. Example: instead of copying credentials between accounts, a build server calls aws sts assume-role to receive a temporary session and then runs SDK calls to deploy application artifacts. The core insight: decouple identity from resource accounts and use temporary sessions to maintain security hygiene.

keyIdea.title: Process summary
keyIdea.text: Create role in target account, set a narrow trust policy, attach permissions, and assume via STS to obtain temporary credentials used by the caller.

content.html:
Process Flow

Cross-account patterns

Three repeatable flows that replace shared credentials.

Centralized security
Security account assumes read-only roles across workload accounts to collect inventories and logs.
CI/CD deployments
Build account pipelines assume deploy roles in target accounts for ephemeral deployment sessions.
Service delegation
Services or automation assume roles to access cross-account resources without storing keys.
Step-by-step flow
  1. Create role in target account and attach permissions policy with least privilege.
  2. Add a trust policy that specifies the exact caller role ARN or service principal.
  3. Caller account invokes STS assume-role and receives temporary credentials.
  4. Use temporary credentials to perform allowed actions and audit usage after expiry.
Example
A pipeline in build account calls assume-role to push application versions to an S3 bucket in the target account without storing any permanent keys.

screens.title: Identity federation: SAML overview
screens.subtitle: How SAML 2.0 enables corporate sign-on to AWS

narration.text: SAML 2.0 is an XML-based standard that lets enterprises use their identity provider to authenticate users and provide assertions to service providers like AWS. In a typical flow, a user signs into the corporate IdP, which issues a SAML assertion asserting the user's identity and attributes. The assertion includes an audience value and is signed by the IdP. AWS exchanges a valid SAML assertion for temporary credentials using sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML, and those credentials are mapped to an IAM role that grants permissions. This avoids creating IAM users for every employee and centralizes authentication, enabling corporate policies such as enforced multi-factor authentication. A concrete example is an employee who logs into the corporate portal, selects an AWS role, and receives temporary console access without an AWS password. A misconception to watch for is treating SAML as a way to bypass IAM permissions; SAML supplies identity and attributes, but the final AWS permissions always come from the attached role. Key takeaway: verify SAML assertions are signed and include the correct audience, and map assertions to minimal, audited roles to maintain least privilege. Identity federation: SAML overview means saml exchanges signed assertions from an idp for temporary aws credentials mapped to an iam role, centralizing authentication.. In practical terms, how saml 2.0 enables corporate sign-on to aws. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SAML purpose
keyIdea.text: SAML exchanges signed assertions from an IdP for temporary AWS credentials mapped to an IAM role, centralizing authentication.

content.html:
SAML 2.0 flow (human users)
IdP authenticates user → IdP issues signed SAML assertion → AWS STS exchanges SAML for temporary credentials mapped to a role.
Trust policy example (SAML)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:saml-provider/YOUR_SAML_PROVIDER_NAME"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "SAML:aud": "https://signin.aws.amazon.com/saml"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Practical checks
  • Ensure the assertion is signed and audience matches AWS SAML endpoint.
  • Map SAML attributes to roles and limit role permissions to minimum required.
  • Enforce IdP-side policies like MFA or conditional access for stronger assurance.
Key Takeaway

SAML centralizes authentication; AWS still enforces permissions through the IAM role attached to the SAML trust.

screens.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC) for machines and apps
screens.subtitle: How OIDC enables application-level federation using JWTs

narration.text: OpenID Connect is an identity layer that builds on OAuth 2.0 and uses JSON Web Tokens to represent authenticated principals. OIDC is suited to machine-to-machine and application federation where services like EKS or serverless functions obtain tokens from an OIDC provider and exchange them for temporary AWS credentials. The provider issues a JWT that contains issuer, audience, expiration, and claims; AWS validates the token against the configured OIDC provider and then allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to provide temporary credentials mapped to an IAM role. A concrete example is a Kubernetes service account that uses an OIDC token to access AWS APIs without storing AWS keys on the pod. A common misconception is that OIDC replaces IAM permissions—OIDC only authenticates; you still attach an IAM role to map identity claims to actions. The practical benefit is stronger security posture and easier keyless authentication for ephemeral workloads. Key design notes: register the OIDC provider in IAM with the correct issuer URL and thumbprint, and be explicit in which claims are accepted when mapping to roles. OpenID Connect (OIDC) for machines and apps means use oidc jwts to authenticate applications and exchange tokens for temporary iam credentials without long-lived keys.. In practical terms, how oidc enables application-level federation using jwts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OIDC purpose
keyIdea.text: Use OIDC JWTs to authenticate applications and exchange tokens for temporary IAM credentials without long-lived keys.

content.html:
OIDC flow for applications
Application obtains a JWT from an OIDC provider → AWS validates the token → sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity returns temporary credentials tied to an IAM role.
Typical use
EKS service accounts and serverless apps that need to call AWS APIs without embedded keys.
Provider setup
Register issuer URL and thumbprint in IAM and configure which token claims you will trust for role mapping.
Concrete example
An EKS pod uses a service account projected token. AWS validates the JWT issuer and audience, then issues temporary AWS credentials to access an S3 bucket the pod needs for processing data.
Common pitfall

Not restricting accepted claims or issuer values can allow tokens from other issuers to be accepted; be explicit about issuer and audience validation.

screens.title: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
screens.subtitle: Using tags to grant permissions dynamically at scale

narration.text: Attribute-Based Access Control shifts permission logic from enumerated roles to tags and attributes attached to principals and resources. Rather than creating a unique role or policy for every combination of team and project, ABAC uses a single policy that compares a principal's tag to a resource's tag at request time. For example, a policy can permit ec2:StartInstances only when the resource tag Project equals the principal's Project tag. This dramatically reduces policy proliferation as projects and teams change. A concrete policy example uses aws:ResourceTag/Project and ${aws:PrincipalTag/Project} inside a StringEquals condition. The primary operational challenge is consistent tagging—mis-tagged resources or principals can produce unintended denial or access. Always combine ABAC with discovery, tagging governance, and testing in the IAM Policy Simulator. Misconceptions include thinking ABAC eliminates the need for least privilege; instead, ABAC should be used to express least-privilege constraints more flexibly. Key takeaway: ABAC simplifies scale when tagging discipline and enforcement are present. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) means grant privileges by matching principal tags to resource tags so policies scale with your tagging strategy.. In practical terms, using tags to grant permissions dynamically at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ABAC in a line
keyIdea.text: Grant privileges by matching principal tags to resource tags so policies scale with your tagging strategy.

content.html:
ABAC policy example
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:StartInstances",
        "ec2:StopInstances"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:ResourceTag/Project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/Project}"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
This policy allows actions only when the resource's Project tag matches the principal's Project tag. Use a single policy to cover many projects and avoid per-project role proliferation.
Governance and checks
  • Enforce tagging standards via automation and resource creation pipelines.
  • Use Policy Simulator to test tag-based conditions before deployment.
  • Monitor mismatches and implement remediation to avoid access failure or over-permission.
Key Takeaway

ABAC greatly reduces policy count when tags are accurate; invest in tagging governance to make ABAC reliable.

screens.title: Cross-account roles vs Federation
screens.subtitle: When to use assume-role versus SAML/OIDC federation

narration.text: It's important to distinguish cross-account roles from federation because they solve related but different problems. Cross-account roles are a resource-account pattern: a role in the trusted account grants temporary permissions to a principal in a trusting account, typically used for programmatic or service-to-service access between accounts you control. Federation uses external identity providers to authenticate users or applications and exchange assertions or tokens for temporary AWS credentials, and is the recommended approach when you want users to sign in with corporate credentials or when external identity platforms issue tokens. For example, a CI/CD pipeline assuming a deploy role across accounts is a cross-account role use case. An employee using a corporate single sign-on portal that issues a SAML assertion to sign into AWS is a federation use case. A misconception is thinking federation replaces IAM roles — in fact federated identities assume IAM roles, so both are combined: federation authenticates the identity, and the IAM role grants permissions. The practical decision: choose cross-account roles for account-to-account delegation you control; choose federation to reuse corporate identity and enforce centralized authentication policies.

keyIdea.title: Decision guide
keyIdea.text: Use cross-account roles for account-level delegation; use federation to authenticate external or corporate identities before mapping them to roles.

content.html:
Comparison

Cross-account roles vs Federation

Both provide temporary credentials, but federation focuses on authentication and identity providers while cross-account roles focus on resource-account delegation.

When to use cross-account roles
Account-to-account automation, pipelines, or service access between accounts you operate.
When to use federation
Human single-sign-on or machine identity from external IdPs like Okta or an OIDC provider.
Side-by-side
Cross-account roles
Resource account defines role; trusting account assumes it via sts:AssumeRole.
Federation
External IdP issues assertion or token; AWS exchanges it for temporary credentials mapped to a role.
Misconception check
Federation does not bypass IAM permissions; it authenticates and then maps identities to IAM roles which determine actions.

screens.title: Hands-on: create a SecurityAuditorRole (scenario)
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step conceptual walkthrough for the hands-on activity

narration.text: We'll walk through the conceptual steps to create SecurityAuditorRole in a workload account that allows a central Security Audit role to assume it and read EC2 resources. Start by choosing the target account and role name. In the workload account, create an IAM role named SecurityAuditorRole and set the trusted entity to the specific ARN of the central auditor role in the audit account. Attach a least-privilege managed policy such as AmazonEC2ReadOnlyAccess, or a custom policy limited to Describe and List actions. Optionally, add an external ID to the trust configuration to prevent confused deputy attacks when third parties are involved. After creating the role, verify from the audit account using the AWS console's Switch Role or the AWS CLI with aws sts assume-role that you can obtain temporary credentials and list EC2 instances. If a permission error occurs, confirm the principal ARN is exact and that the role's permissions policy permits the read operations. This exercise demonstrates how trust policies and permissions policies combine to produce secure, temporary cross-account access. Hands-on: create a SecurityAuditorRole (scenario) means create a role in the workload account permitting a specific auditor role to assume it with read-only ec2 permissions, and verify assume-role works.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal

content.html:
Core Concept

Hands-on: SecurityAuditorRole

Conceptual steps to provision and verify a cross-account auditor role.

Role creation steps
  1. In workload account (444455556666) create role named SecurityAuditorRole.
  2. Set trusted entity to arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/CentralSecurityAuditor.
  3. Attach AmazonEC2ReadOnlyAccess or equivalent read-only policy.
  4. Optionally require an external ID for extra protection.
Verification
From the audit account, assume the CentralSecurityAuditor role and attempt to list EC2 instances in the workload account. Confirm listing succeeds and modify attempts are denied.
Note: Using exact role ARNs and optional external IDs reduces the chance of unintended assume operations.
CLI example (conceptual)
# From the audit account, assume role in workload account
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/SecurityAuditorRole --role-session-name AuditSession

# Use returned temporary credentials to list instances in workload account
aws ec2 describe-instances --region us-east-1

screens.title: Common IAM mistakes and mitigations
screens.subtitle: Identify risky policies and trust relationships and how to fix them

narration.text: Understanding common IAM mistakes helps you avoid security incidents. Frequent errors include granting wildcards for Actions or Resources, granting Allow on NotResource, and using overly broad Principals in trust policies such as account root or the wildcard Principal. These mistakes can allow privilege escalation or unintended account access. For cross-account roles, an overly permissive trust policy—Principal: { "AWS": "*" }—is especially dangerous because it allows any principal to attempt assume-role, relying only on conditions to limit usage. Mitigations include auditing trust policies, replacing account-level Principals with specific role ARNs, enabling external IDs for third-party delegation, requiring MFA where appropriate, and applying permissions boundaries to limit the maximum permissions a delegated identity can receive. For federation, ensure assertions and tokens are signed and validate audience fields; for ABAC, invest in tagging governance and use the Policy Simulator to validate tag-based policies. The key point is that explicit, narrow policies combined with automation for tagging and auditing reduce risk and make incidents easier to investigate. Common IAM mistakes and mitigations means replace broad principals with explicit arns, require external ids/mfa where appropriate, enforce tagging governance, and use permissions boundaries and audits.. In practical terms, identify risky policies and trust relationships and how to fix them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fixes to apply
keyIdea.text: Replace broad Principals with explicit ARNs, require external IDs/MFA where appropriate, enforce tagging governance, and use permissions boundaries and audits.

content.html:
Common mistakes
  • Using "*" for Action or Resource in permissions policies.
  • Trust policies that allow account root or wildcard Principals.
  • Not validating SAML assertions or OIDC token issuers and audiences.
  • Inconsistent tagging causing ABAC failures or unintended access.
Mitigations
  • Audit and tighten Principals to specific role ARNs.
  • Require external IDs for third-party assume-role scenarios.
  • Use permissions boundaries for delegated admin roles.
  • Automate tagging and test ABAC policies with the Policy Simulator.
Scenario: risky trust policy
If a role's trust policy uses Principal: { "AWS": "*" }, an attacker who can obtain any AWS credentials may attempt to assume that role. Fix by specifying the exact ARN of the trusting role or the federated provider, and add Conditions like external ID or source IP when useful.
Warning

Broad trust and permission policies are a common root cause of privilege escalation. Narrow and verify frequently.

screens.title: CLI assume-role demo (conceptual)
screens.subtitle: Using aws sts assume-role to obtain temporary credentials — conceptual example

narration.text: A practical demonstration often begins in the trusting account with the caller's IAM role or user requesting temporary credentials from STS. The AWS CLI supports an assume-role call that returns temporary credentials which you then export into your environment for subsequent A P I calls. Conceptually, you run aws sts assume-role with the role ARN and a session name. STS returns AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken with a limited duration. Then you use those credentials to call services like listing S3 buckets or describing EC2 instances in the trusted account. This flow avoids permanent credentials and gives auditable, time-limited sessions. A common error is copying returned credentials into long-term profiles; instead use ephemeral sessions or short-lived environment variables for immediate actions. When testing, verify the returned credentials permit only the intended read or write actions. This CLI pattern is a simple and repeatable way to validate cross-account and federated workflows during development and audits. CLI assume-role demo (conceptual) means use aws sts assume-role to request temporary credentials, use them for a short operation, and avoid storing them long-term.. In practical terms, using aws sts assume-role to obtain temporary credentials — conceptual example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CLI pattern
keyIdea.text: Use aws sts assume-role to request temporary credentials, use them for a short operation, and avoid storing them long-term.

content.html:
Conceptual CLI snippet
# Assume the role and capture temporary credentials
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/SecurityAuditorRole --role-session-name AuditSession

# The command returns AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken and Expiration. Use them for subsequent calls:
# aws s3 ls --profile temp-session
Remember: do not hard-code returned credentials. Use them for immediate, auditable tasks and rely on session expiry to limit exposure.
Example verification
After assuming the role, try listing resources the role should see. If listing succeeds but write operations fail, the role is correctly scoped to read-only.
Key Takeaway

Use the CLI as a repeatable validation tool: assume, test allowed actions, and ensure denied actions remain blocked.

narration.text: Here are compact reminders of the core concepts you've seen. IAM roles for cross-account access let a principal in one account assume a role in another using STS, producing temporary, auditable credentials. Identity federation connects external IdPs so users can sign in with existing corporate credentials; SAML is common for human sign-on and exchanges signed assertions for role-based access. OIDC is used for machine or application identity where JWTs are validated and exchanged for temporary credentials. These foundational ideas work together: federation authenticates identities, cross-account roles grant scoped permissions, and STS issues the temporary credentials that tie it all together. Keep these concise definitions in mind as you design secure, scalable access in multi-account environments. Key Concepts — Part 1 means trust, authentication, and temporary credentials are the pillars of secure cross-account and federated access.. In practical terms, essential definitions and short explanations. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Summary strip
keyIdea.text: Trust, authentication, and temporary credentials are the pillars of secure cross-account and federated access.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 1
IAM Roles for Cross-Account Access
Allow a principal in one account to assume a role in another and use temporary permissions.
Identity Federation
Use external IdPs so users can access AWS with corporate credentials instead of IAM users.
SAML 2.0
XML assertions from an IdP are exchanged for temporary AWS credentials mapped to an IAM role.
Summary

Authentication, trust policies, and temporary credentials form a secure chain for cross-account and federated access.

narration.text: These final reminders focus on ABAC, STS, trust policies and permissions boundaries. ABAC lets you write a single policy that grants access when principal and resource tags match, which is powerful when tags are consistent. AWS Security Token Service issues temporary credentials for assumed roles or federated sessions—these credentials expire and reduce the risk of leaked long-term keys. A trust policy defines which principals may assume a role; make it explicit and narrow. Permissions boundaries let you set an upper bound on what a role or user can receive even if their policies attempt to grant greater breadth. Together, these tools enable secure, scalable access management when combined with tagging governance, regular audits, and careful condition checks like external IDs and audience validation. Keep auditing trust relationships and avoid broad Principals or wildcard policies.

keyIdea.title: Closing takeaway
keyIdea.text: Combine ABAC, narrow trust policies, STS temporary sessions, and permissions boundaries to build secure, scalable IAM architectures.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 2
ABAC
Tag-driven policies reduce the need for many role permutations when tagging is enforced.
AWS STS
Issues temporary credentials for assumed roles or federated sessions; they expire and reduce credential risk.
Permissions Boundary
Set the maximum permissions a role or user can receive, limiting the blast radius of delegated policies.
Final takeaway

Design narrow trust policies, validate federation assertions, govern tagging, and rely on STS sessions to keep access temporary and auditable.
